## OWASP — Open Web Application Security Project *OWASP* is a worldwide nonprofit that publishes freely‑available resources to improve the security of software. The organization is best known for its **OWASP Top 10**, a community‑derived list that highlights the most critical web‑application security risks. --- ## What the OWASP Top 10 Is | Item | What it means | Why it matters | |------|---------------|----------------| | **Purpose** | A high‑level, globally‑recognised reference for **what to protect against** in web applications. | Helps developers, architects, QA, and security teams prioritise security controls and testing. | | **Audience** | Developers, testers, security professionals, product managers, and executives. | Gives a common language for risk discussions. | | **Format** | A ranked list of ten security categories (each with a brief description, example attacks, and mitigations). | Prioritises effort: the top 5 are usually the biggest risks to fix first. | | **Update cycle** | Every 3 years (previous: 2003, 2005, 2007, 2008, 2010, 2013, 2014, 2017, 2021, **2023**). | Reflects evolving threat landscapes, new vulnerabilities, and community input. | | **Methodology** | • Community surveys (security professionals, vendors, researchers)
• Threat‑modeling
• Data‑driven analysis (CVEs, bug‑bounty reports, penetration‑testing logs)
• Expert workshops | Ensures that the list is evidence‑based and globally representative. | --- ## The OWASP Top 10 (2023 Edition) > *(If you’re reading this after 2023 you’ll probably see the 2023 list. The 2021 edition is still widely referenced, but the 2023 release includes a few category changes.)* | Rank | Category | Short Name | Key Concepts | Typical Examples | Common Mitigations | |------|----------|------------|--------------|------------------|--------------------| | 1 | **A01:2023 – Broken Access Control** | Access control failures | Users can act beyond their permissions. | An API that lets a user read another user’s private data. | Principle of least privilege; enforce role‑based access; secure session management. | | 2 | **A02:2023 – Cryptographic Failures** | Crypto failures | Sensitive data not properly protected in transit or at rest. | Plain‑text passwords stored, weak TLS configuration. | Use strong, modern cryptography; secure key management; enforce TLS 1.2+/TLS 1.3. | | 3 | **A03:2023 – Injection** | Injection attacks | Untrusted data is inserted into a query or command. | SQLi, NoSQLi, OS command injection, LDAP injection. | Parameterised queries, ORMs, input validation, whitelisting. | | 4 | **A04:2023 – Insecure Design** | Design‑level gaps | The architecture itself is missing security controls. | No threat modeling, no authentication flow review. | Threat modeling, secure design principles, security by design. | | 5 | **A05:2023 – Security Misconfiguration** | Misconfigurations | Default settings or missing hardening steps expose the app. | Unrestricted cloud storage, open admin consoles, default credentials. | Harden infrastructure, enforce least‑privilege configs, automated configuration checks. | | 6 | **A06:2023 – Vulnerable and Outdated Components** | Known‑vulnerability libraries | Third‑party libs contain exploitable bugs. | Using an old version of a CMS with a known XSS flaw. | Keep dependencies up‑to‑date, use dependency‑scan tools, CVE monitoring. | | 7 | **A07:2023 – Identification and Authentication Failures** | Auth failures | Weaknesses in authentication allow bypass or credential compromise. | Credential stuffing, weak MFA, session fixation. | Strong password policies, MFA, secure session tokens, rate limiting. | | 8 | **A08:2023 – Software and Data Integrity Failures** | Integrity failures | Code or data is tampered with, or integrity checks are missing. | Malicious build pipelines, unverified third‑party data. | Code signing, secure CI/CD pipelines, hash verification. | | 9 | **A09:2023 – Security Logging and Monitoring Failures** | Poor observability | Attackers remain hidden because logging is inadequate. | No audit trail for failed logins, no alerting on suspicious activity. | Centralised logging, immutable logs, SIEM integration, alerting. | |10 | **A10:2023 – Server‑Side Request Forgery (SSRF)** | SSRF | The server can be made to request arbitrary URLs. | Unrestricted HTTP client that can be exploited to read internal services. | Validate/whitelist outbound URLs, network segmentation, request sandboxing. | > **Note:** > *The 2023 edition removed “A05 – Security Misconfiguration” and “A07 – Identification and Authentication Failures” as separate categories, consolidating them into broader themes. The new “Server‑Side Request Forgery” (SSRF) reflects the growing prevalence of cloud‑native attacks.* --- ## How to Use the OWASP Top 10 | Stage | What to do | Practical Steps | |-------|------------|-----------------| | **Risk Assessment** | Identify which categories affect your app. | Map your features to categories; score risk based on severity and likelihood. | | **Threat Modeling** | Model how each category could be exploited. | Run STRIDE or PASTA analyses; create attack trees. | | **Secure Coding** | Incorporate mitigations from the start. | Follow secure‑coding guidelines (e.g., OWASP Secure Coding Practices). | | **Testing & QA** | Verify that mitigations work. | Use unit tests, static analysis, dynamic scanning, manual pentest. | | **Deployment & Ops** | Harden the environment. | Automate configuration checks (e.g., with IaC linting); use hardening guides. | | **Monitoring & Response** | Detect breaches early. | Enable logging, set up alerts, perform incident‑response drills. | | **Continuous Improvement** | Iterate with new OWASP editions. | Track compliance, keep dependencies fresh, re‑test after updates. | --- ## Quick Reference Cheat‑Sheet | Category | Symptom | Fix | |----------|---------|-----| | Broken Access | Unauthorized API access | Enforce role‑based checks; validate access on every request | | Crypto | Data in transit/stored in clear text | TLS 1.3, HSTS, encryption libraries, secure key vaults | | Injection | SQL/NoSQL errors, command execution | Parameterised queries, input sanitisation | | Insecure Design | No threat modeling | Conduct design reviews; adopt security design patterns | | Misconfiguration | Open admin UI, default creds | Harden settings, use automation to apply patches | | Vulnerable Components | CVE‑2023‑xxxx in lib | Update, use dependency‑scanning | | Auth Failures | Password reuse, weak MFA | Enforce MFA, lockout policies, session management | | Integrity | Malicious code in build | Signed artefacts, pipeline security | | Logging | No audit trail | Centralised logs, immutable storage | | SSRF | Internal service exposed via URL | Validate outbound URLs, network segmentation | --- ## Resources | Resource | Why It’s Helpful | |----------|-----------------| | **OWASP Top 10 Official Site** – https://owasp.org/www-project-top-ten/ | Full list, methodology, guidance. | | **OWASP Cheat Sheets** – https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/ | Detailed mitigations for each category. | | **OWASP AppSec Conferences** – https://owasp.org/events/ | Latest research, case studies. | | **OWASP Dependency‑Check** – https://owasp.org/www-project-dependency-check/ | Automated vulnerability scanning for dependencies. | | **OWASP ZAP / Burp Suite** | Dynamic testing tools for injection, auth, SSRF, etc. | --- ### Bottom line The **OWASP Top 10** is *not* a checklist of “things you must do” but a **prioritised reference** of the most pressing web‑application vulnerabilities. By aligning your development lifecycle—design, code, test, deploy, and monitor—around these categories, you give your organization the best shot at staying ahead of the most common—and often most costly—security pitfalls.
